claim: Inhibition of infralimbic cortex (IL), irrespective of its intrinsic neural activity, attenuates the ability of environmental cues predictive of reward availability to promote reward seeking.
source: Inhibition of IL, irrespective of its intrinsic neural activity, attenuates not only the ability of environmental cues predictive of reward availability to promote reward seeking, but also the ability of environmental cues predictive of reward omission to suppress this behavior.
evidence: This claim is presented as established knowledge in the abstract, setting up the context for the study.

claim: Inhibition of infralimbic cortex (IL), irrespective of its intrinsic neural activity, attenuates the ability of environmental cues predictive of reward omission to suppress reward seeking behavior.
source: Inhibition of IL, irrespective of its intrinsic neural activity, attenuates not only the ability of environmental cues predictive of reward availability to promote reward seeking, but also the ability of environmental cues predictive of reward omission to suppress this behavior.
evidence: This claim is presented as established knowledge in the abstract, setting up the context for the study.

claim: Bidirectional behavioral modulation in rats is mediated by functionally distinct units of neurons (neural ensembles) that are concurrently localized within the same IL brain area but selectively reactive to different environmental cues.
source: Here we report that such bidirectional behavioral modulation in rats is mediated by functionally distinct units of neurons (neural ensembles) that are concurrently localized within the same IL brain area but selectively reactive to different environmental cues.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Ensemble-specific neural activity is thought to function as a memory engram representing a learned association between environment and behavior.
source: Ensemble-specific neural activity is thought to function as a memory engram representing a learned association between environment and behavior.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific consensus about neural ensembles and memory engrams.

claim: Two distinct engrams exist concurrently within the infralimbic cortex, each mediating opposing environmental actions on a learned behavior.
source: Our findings establish the causal evidence for the concurrent existence of two distinct engrams within a single brain site, each mediating opposing environmental actions on a learned behavior.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data showing selective disruption effects.

claim: Different units of neurons or 'neural ensembles' within a single brain area selectively react to different environmental cues, as shown by electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies.
source: Different units of neurons or 'neural ensembles' (Eichenbaum, 1993) within a single brain area selectively react to different environmental cues, as shown by electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies (e.g., Schoenbaum et al., 1998; Jog et al., 1999; Frank et al., 2000; Ohki et al., 2005; Komiyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies.

claim: Ensemble-specific brain activity is thought to function as the memory engram, each representing a unique learned association between environment and behavior.
source: Such ensemble-specific brain activity is thought to function as the memory engram, each representing a unique learned association between environment and behavior (Cruz et al., 2013; Mayford, 2014; Tonegawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work on memory engrams.

claim: It is commonly thought that multiple engrams concurrently exist within a single brain site at a single stage of learning based on correlational evidence from electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies.
source: Based on the correlational evidence from electrophysiological and calcium imaging studies, it is commonly thought that multiple engrams concurrently exist within a single brain site at a single stage of learning.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific consensus based on correlational studies.

claim: Previous studies have established the causal evidence that a single brain area or ensemble can represent two different engrams at two different stages of learning.
source: Previous studies have established the causal evidence that a single brain area (Warren et al., 2016) or ensemble (Redondo et al., 2014) can represent two different engrams at two different stages of learning (e.g., before vs. after extinction training).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous causal studies.

claim: The causal evidence supporting the concurrent existence of multiple engrams within a single brain site, each mediating different environmental actions on a learned behavior, is still lacking.
source: However, the causal evidence supporting the concurrent existence of multiple engrams within a single brain site, each mediating different environmental actions on a learned behavior (e.g., a go/no-go task), is still lacking.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in the scientific literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The study presents causal evidence for the concurrent existence of two distinct engrams within the infralimbic cortex (IL) of rats, each mediating opposing environmental actions on a pre-established operant response.
source: Here we present the causal evidence for the concurrent existence of two distinct engrams within the infralimbic cortex (IL) of rats, each mediating opposing environmental actions on a pre-established operant response.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: The findings help reconcile contradictory reports regarding the role of IL in the environmental control of appetitive behavior.
source: Our findings help reconcile the contradictory reports regarding the role of IL in the environmental control of appetitive behavior (Gourley and Taylor, 2016).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the study's implications for resolving conflicting literature.

claim: Non-selective disruption of IL prevents promotion of reward seeking by cues signaling reward availability.
source: Some reports (Koya et al., 2009a; Bossert et al., 2011) indicate that non-selective disruption of IL, irrespective of neural activity, prevents promotion of reward seeking by cues signaling reward availability (e.g., reward contexts).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from previous studies cited.

claim: Non-selective disruption of IL prevents suppression of reward seeking by cues signaling reward omission.
source: However, other reports (Peters et al., 2008; LaLumiere et al., 2012) indicate that non-selective disruption of IL prevents suppression of reward seeking by cues signaling reward omission (e.g., extinction contexts).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from previous studies cited.

claim: Non-selective disruption of IL has no significant effect on either promotion or suppression of reward seeking.
source: Yet other reports (Willcocks and McNally, 2013; Pfarr et al., 2015) indicate that the non-selective disruption of IL has no significant effect on either promotion or suppression of reward seeking.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from previous studies cited.

claim: The discrepancies in previous reports could be the results of different IL neurons selectively reacting to different cues signaling reward availability and omission.
source: These discrepancies could be the results of different IL neurons selectively reacting to different cues signaling reward availability and omission.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain conflicting literature.

claim: Distinct neural ensembles – concurrently existing within IL but each selectively reactive to a discriminative stimulus predictive of reward availability (S+) or omission (S-) – differentially control promotion and suppression of reward seeking.
source: We hypothesized that distinct neural ensembles – concurrently existing within IL but each selectively reactive to a discriminative stimulus predictive of reward availability (S+) or omission (S-) – differentially control promotion and suppression of reward seeking.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study that was tested experimentally.

claim: All rats were trained to recognize three sets of cues predictive of rewards at varying probability: active lever and light-cue (50%), S+ (100%) and S- (0%).
source: All rats were trained to recognize three sets of cues predictive of rewards at varying probability: active lever and light-cue (50%), S+ (100%) and S- (0%).
evidence: This describes the experimental training procedure used in the study.

claim: All rats were trained to lever-press for a sweet solution containing 3% glucose and 0.125% saccharin presented together with a light-cue.
source: All rats were trained to lever-press for a sweet solution (containing 3% glucose and 0.125% saccharin) presented together with a light-cue (Figure 1A)
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and references Figure 1A showing the training data.

claim: All rats were trained to recognize distinct auditory cues (white noise and beeping tone) as S+ and S-.
source: and further trained to recognize distinct auditory cues (white noise and beeping tone) as S+ and S- (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and references Figure 1B showing the discrimination training data.

claim: Each rat underwent three cue-tests for bidirectional environmental modulation of reward seeking: (1) active lever and light-cue without S+ or S- ('No S+/S-'), (2) active lever, light-cue and S+, (3) active lever, light-cue and S-.
source: Each rat underwent three cue-tests (Figure 2A) for bidirectional environmental modulation of reward seeking: (1) active lever and light-cue without S+ or S- ('No S+/S-'), (2) active lever, light-cue and S+, (3) active lever, light-cue and S-.
evidence: This describes the experimental testing procedure and references Figure 2A.

claim: Glucose and saccharin were not available during the cue-tests.
source: Glucose and saccharin were not available during these tests.
evidence: This describes a specific condition of the experimental procedure.

claim: One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) on active lever-pressing revealed a significant effect of cue-test (F(2,89) = 216.679, p<0.001).
source: One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) on active lever-pressing revealed a significant effect of cue-test (F(2,89) = 216.679, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The active lever and light-cue sufficiently initiated and maintained lever-pressing.
source: The active lever and light-cue sufficiently initiated and maintained lever-pressing (see No S+/S-).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, referencing the No S+/S- condition in Figure 2A.

claim: In each animal, superimposing S+ significantly potentiated lever-pressing (p<0.001).
source: In each animal, superimposing S+ significantly potentiated lever-pressing (p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Superimposing S- significantly suppressed lever-pressing behavior (p<0.001).
source: while superimposing S- significantly suppressed this behavior (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The bidirectional environmental modulation of reward seeking is presumably mediated by learning processes known as 'conditioned excitation or inhibition' or 'positive or negative occasion setting'.
source: This bidirectional environmental modulation of reward seeking is presumably mediated by learning processes known as 'conditioned excitation or inhibition' (Rescorla, 1969) or 'positive or negative occasion setting' (Schmajuk et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results based on established learning theory concepts, supported by citations.

claim: The rats were randomly divided into four groups defined by disruption-cue (S+ or S-) and microinjection (Daun02 or vehicle) for neural activity-targeted inactivation.
source: The rats were then randomly divided into four groups defined by disruption-cue (S+ or S-) and microinjection (Daun02 or vehicle) for neural activity-targeted inactivation (Figure 2B) using previously established procedures (Koya et al., 2009b; Bossert et al., 2011; Pfarr et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and references Figure 2B and previous methodological studies.

claim: Each rat was exposed to either S+ or S-, and then received a bilateral microinjection of Daun02 (2.0 µg/0.5 µl/side) or vehicle (0.5 µl/side) into IL.
source: Each rat was first exposed to either S+ or S-, and then received a bilateral microinjection of Daun02 (2.0 µg/0.5 µl/side) or vehicle (0.5 µl/side) into IL.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for the Daun02 disruption.

claim: In Fos-lacZ rats, Daun02 (inactive compound) is catalyzed into daunorubicin (cytotoxin) by beta-galactosidase (enzyme) only in 'activated' cells expressing Fos (activation marker), thereby triggering apoptosis.
source: In Fos-lacZ rats, Daun02 (inactive compound) is catalyzed into daunorubicin (cytotoxin) by beta-galactosidase (enzyme) only in 'activated' cells expressing Fos (activation marker), thereby triggering apoptosis (see Pfarr et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the Daun02 technique, supported by a citation.

claim: Daun02 cannot be catalyzed into daunorubicin in 'non-activated' cells lacking Fos expression (and thus beta-galactosidase), and cellular disruption is prevented.
source: In contrast, Daun02 cannot be catalyzed into daunorubicin in 'non-activated' cells lacking Fos expression (and thus beta-galactosidase), and cellular disruption is prevented.
evidence: This describes the selectivity mechanism of the Daun02 technique.

claim: Daun02 selectively inactivates Fos-positive 'activated' neurons without disrupting the surrounding Fos-negative 'non-activated' neurons.
source: As such, Daun02 selectively inactivates Fos-positive 'activated' neurons without disrupting the surrounding Fos-negative 'non-activated' neurons.
evidence: This summarizes the selectivity of the Daun02 technique.

claim: On the day of Daun02 disruption, both active lever and light-cue were not introduced, thus the rats were withheld from lever-pressing, as to not disrupt neurons activated by either active lever or light-cue.
source: On the day of Daun02 disruption, both active lever and light-cue were not introduced. Thus, the rats were withheld from lever-pressing, as to not disrupt neurons activated by either active lever or light-cue.
evidence: This describes a specific control condition in the experimental procedure.

claim: Three-way ANOVA on active lever-press revealed significant effects of disruption-cue (F(1,86) = 8.839, p<0.01), cue-test (F(2,172) = 313.899, p<0.001), and significant interactions for disruption-cue and microinjection (F(1,86) = 5.87, p<0.05), disruption-cue and cue-test (F(2,172) = 9.694, p<0.001), microinjection and cue-test (F(2,172) = 22.936, p<0.001), and disruption-cue and microinjection and cue-test (F(2,172) = 6.172, p<0.01).
source: Three-way ANOVA on active lever-press revealed significant effects of disruption-cue (F(1,86) = 8.839, p<0.01), cue-test (F(2,172) = 313.899, p<0.001), and significant interactions for disruption-cue and microinjection (F(1,86) = 5.87, p<0.05), disruption-cue and cue-test (F(2,172) = 9.694, p<0.001), microinjection and cue-test (F(2,172) = 22.936, p<0.001), and disruption-cue and microinjection and cue-test (F(2,172) = 6.172, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the post-disruption test data analysis.

claim: In the two vehicle-treated control groups ('S+ & vehicle' and 'S- & vehicle'), the bidirectional modulation of lever-pressing by S+ or S- was evident (p<0.01–0.001).
source: In the two vehicle-treated control groups ('S+ & vehicle' and 'S- & vehicle'), the bidirectional modulation of lever-pressing by S+ or S- was evident (p<0.01–0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the post-disruption test data analysis for control groups.

claim: In the group that received Daun02 following exposure to S+ ('S+ & Daun02'), Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S+ blocked the promotion of lever-pressing by S+ but spared the suppression of this behavior by S- (p<0.01).
source: In the group that received Daun02 following exposure to S+ ('S+ & Daun02'), Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S+ blocked the promotion of lever-pressing by S+ but spared the suppression of this behavior by S- (p<0.01).
evidence: This is a key experimental result showing selective disruption of S+ ensemble function.

claim: In the group that received Daun02 following exposure to S- ('S- & Daun02'), Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S- blocked suppression by S- but spared promotion by S+ (p<0.01).
source: In the group that received Daun02 following exposure to S- ('S- & Daun02'), Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S- blocked suppression by S- but spared promotion by S+ (p<0.01).
evidence: This is a key experimental result showing selective disruption of S- ensemble function.

claim: For all cases, basal lever-pressing initiated and maintained by active lever and light-cue was not significantly altered by Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S+ or S-.
source: For all cases, basal lever-pressing initiated and maintained by active lever and light-cue was not significantly altered by Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S+ or S- (see No S+/S-).
evidence: This is an important control result showing specificity of the disruption effects, referencing the No S+/S- condition in Figure 2C.

claim: Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by either S+ or S- exclusively altered the cue-modulation of reward seeking uniquely linked to the targeted cue in a single animal.
source: Thus, Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by either S+ or S- exclusively altered the cue-modulation of reward seeking uniquely linked to the targeted cue in a single animal.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral data showing selective disruption effects.

claim: Daun02's effect on disrupting neural ensemble activity was verified by Fos immunohistochemistry using previously established procedures.
source: Daun02's effect on disrupting neural ensemble activity was verified by Fos immunohistochemistry (Figure 3) using previously established procedures (Koya et al., 2009b; Bossert et al., 2011; Pfarr et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the verification method and references Figure 3 and previous methodological studies.

claim: Each of the four groups prepared for the Daun02 disruption was further divided into three groups defined by the final Fos-induction conditions ('S+', 'S-' or 'No S+/S-').
source: Each of the four groups prepared for the Daun02 disruption was further divided into three groups defined by the final Fos-induction conditions ('S+', 'S-' or 'No S+/S-').
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the Fos immunohistochemistry verification.

claim: Active lever and light-cue were not introduced during the final Fos-induction in order to determine IL ensembles specifically reactive to S+ or S-.
source: However, active lever and light-cue were not introduced in order to determine IL ensembles specifically reactive to S+ or S-.
evidence: This describes a specific control condition in the Fos verification procedure.

claim: Three-way ANOVA on Fos-positive nuclei in IL revealed significant effects of microinjection (F(1,78) = 7.695, p<0.01), Fos-induction (F(2,78) = 31.129, p<0.001), and significant interactions for disruption-cue and Fos-induction (F(2,78) = 14.803, p<0.001), disruption-cue and microinjection and Fos-induction (F(2,78) = 11.016, p<0.001).
source: Three-way ANOVA on Fos-positive nuclei in IL revealed significant effects of microinjection (F(1,78) = 7.695, p<0.01), Fos-induction (F(2,78) = 31.129, p<0.001), and significant interactions for disruption-cue and Fos-induction (F(2,78) = 14.803, p<0.001), disruption-cue and microinjection and Fos-induction (F(2,78) = 11.016, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Fos immunohistochemistry data analysis.

claim: In the two vehicle-treated control groups ('S+ & vehicle' and 'S- & vehicle'), both S+ and S- significantly increased Fos-positive nuclei in IL (Ps < 0.05–0.01).
source: In the two vehicle-treated control groups ('S+ & vehicle' and 'S- & vehicle'), both S+ and S- significantly increased Fos-positive nuclei in IL (Ps < 0.05–0.01).
evidence: This is a result from the Fos immunohistochemistry data analysis for control groups.

claim: In the group that received Daun02 following exposure to S+ ('S+ & Daun02'), Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S+ prevented the induction of Fos by S+ but spared the induction by S- (p<0.05).
source: In the group that received Daun02 following exposure to S+ ('S+ & Daun02'), Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S+ prevented the induction of Fos by S+ but spared the induction by S- (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a key result from the Fos immunohistochemistry showing selective disruption of S+ ensemble.

claim: In the group that received Daun02 following exposure to S- ('S- & Daun02'), Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S- significantly reduced the induction of Fos by S- but spared the induction by S+ (p<0.05).
source: In the group that received Daun02 following exposure to S- ('S- & Daun02'), Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by S- significantly reduced the induction of Fos by S- but spared the induction by S+ (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a key result from the Fos immunohistochemistry showing selective disruption of S- ensemble.

claim: Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by either S+ or S- exclusively altered the cue-triggered neural activation uniquely linked to the targeted cue in a single animal.
source: Thus, Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by either S+ or S- exclusively altered the cue-triggered neural activation uniquely linked to the targeted cue in a single animal.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the Fos immunohistochemistry data showing selective disruption effects.

claim: The same IL brain area is capable of controlling both promotion and suppression of reward seeking via different neural ensembles, each selectively reactive to S+ or S-.
source: Together with a recent electrophysiological report (Moorman and Aston-Jones, 2015), our findings establish that the same IL brain area is capable of controlling both promotion and suppression of reward seeking via different neural ensembles, each selectively reactive to S+ or S-.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study, integrating the current findings with previous electrophysiological work.

claim: Mutually exclusive rather than overlapping neural ensembles in IL likely mediate the bidirectional environmental control of reward seeking.
source: Because Daun02 disruption of IL neurons activated by either S+ or S- exclusively altered the behavioral response (Figure 2) as well as neural activation (Figure 3) uniquely linked to the targeted cue, mutually exclusive rather than overlapping neural ensembles in IL likely mediate the bidirectional environmental control of reward seeking.
evidence: This is an inference from the selective disruption effects observed in both behavioral and neural data.

claim: The current results demonstrate the functional significance of manipulating brain cells based on their activity in addition to other characteristics, such as locality and phenotype.
source: As is the case of recent studies that utilized similar activity-dependent procedures (e.g., Redondo et al., 2014; Grosso et al., 2015), the current results demonstrate the functional significance of manipulating brain cells based on their activity in addition to other characteristics, such as locality and phenotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the methodological implications of the study, supported by citations to similar approaches.

claim: Caution should be raised to the use of non-selective techniques that manipulate neural activity irrespective of intrinsic neural activity for determining the brain behavioral functions.
source: We thus raise caution to the use of non-selective techniques that manipulate neural activity irrespective of intrinsic neural activity for determining the brain behavioral functions.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: The findings provide the causal evidence for the concurrent existence of multiple engrams, each mediating different and even opposing environmental actions on a behavior, in a single brain area.
source: Finally, our findings provide the causal evidence for the concurrent existence of multiple engrams, each mediating different and even opposing environmental actions on a behavior, in a single brain area.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing the causal evidence provided.

claim: Ensemble-specific neural phenotype as well as both local and brain-wide neurocircuitry involving each unique engram should be elucidated in future studies.
source: In light of recent studies implicating differential brain processes in differential environmental control of a learned response (Ciocchi et al., 2010; Trouche et al., 2013; Adhikari et al., 2015), ensemble-specific neural phenotype as well as both local and brain-wide neurocircuitry involving each unique engram should be elucidated in future studies.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the current findings and related literature.

claim: A total of one hundred nineteen male Fos-lacZ transgenic rats on a Sprague-Dawley background were used.
source: A total of one hundred nineteen male Fos-lacZ transgenic rats (Kasof et al., 1995) on a Sprague-Dawley background were used (RRID:SCR_014785).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: A total of ninety rats were retained for statistical analyses.
source: Of which, a total of ninety rats were retained for statistical analyses (see below).
evidence: This describes the final sample size after exclusions.

claim: The Fos-lacZ transgenic strain is required for neural activity-targeted disruption of neural ensembles by Daun02 pharmacogenetic inactivation.
source: This transgenic strain is required for neural activity-targeted disruption of neural ensembles by Daun02 pharmacogenetic inactivation (Koya et al., 2009b).
evidence: This explains the rationale for using this specific transgenic strain, supported by a citation.

claim: All rats were bred at The Scripps Research Institute, and genotyped by Laragen, Inc.
source: All rats were bred at The Scripps Research Institute, and genotyped by Laragen, Inc. (Culver City, CA).
evidence: This describes the source and genotyping of the animals.

claim: The rats were group-housed (two rats per cage) in plastic cages in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, maintained on a 12 hr/12 hr reverse light/dark cycle (lights on at 20:00 hr).
source: The rats were group-housed (two rats per cage) in plastic cages in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, maintained on a 12 hr/12 hr reverse light/dark cycle (lights on at 20:00 hr).
evidence: This describes the housing conditions for the animals.

claim: At all times, the rats were allowed free access to food and water.
source: At all times, the rats were allowed free access to food and water.
evidence: This describes the feeding conditions for the animals.

claim: All Fos-lacZ rats (250–300 g) were surgically implanted with permanent bilateral guide cannulae (22 G; Plastics One, Roanoke, VA, USA) under isoflurane anesthesia for the microinjection of Daun02 or vehicle into the infralimibic cortex (IL).
source: All Fos-lacZ rats (250–300 g) were surgically implanted with permanent bilateral guide cannulae (22 G; Plastics One, Roanoke, VA, USA) under isoflurane anesthesia for the microinjection of Daun02 or vehicle (see below) into the infralimibic cortex (IL).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: The microinjection coordinates were anteroposterior + 3.2 mm, mediolateral ± 0.6 mm, dorsoventral −5.5 mm.
source: The microinjection coordinates were anteroposterior + 3.2 mm, mediolateral ± 0.6 mm, dorsoventral −5.5 mm.
evidence: This provides the specific stereotaxic coordinates used for IL targeting.

claim: Rats were allowed to recover at least seven days before the start of the behavioral procedures.
source: Rats were allowed to recover at least seven days before the start of the behavioral procedures (see below).
evidence: This describes the recovery period after surgery.

claim: One rat died during the surgery, and five rats died due to post-operation complications.
source: One rat died during the surgery, and five rats died due to post-operation complications.
evidence: This reports attrition during the surgical phase.

claim: The animal model for the bidirectional modulation of reward seeking by discriminative stimuli predictive of reward availability (S+) and reward omission (S-) was developed.
source: We developed an animal model for the bidirectional modulation of reward seeking by discriminative stimuli predictive of reward availability (S+) and reward omission (S-).
evidence: This describes the novel behavioral model developed for the study.

claim: The behavioral model consisted of twelve experimental phases and lasted over six months.
source: This model consisted of twelve experimental phases and lasted over six months.
evidence: This describes the duration and complexity of the behavioral model.

claim: The rats were always trained and tested during the dark (active) phase in a dedicated operant conditioning chamber equipped with two retractable levers (one 'active lever' and one 'inactive lever'), a 'light-cue' and a drinking well.
source: The rats were always trained and tested during the dark (active) phase in a dedicated operant conditioning chamber ('chamber') equipped with two retractable levers (one 'active lever' and one 'inactive lever'), a 'light-cue' and a drinking well.
evidence: This describes the testing conditions and apparatus.

claim: Insertion of both active and inactive levers signaled the start of a once daily operant conditioning session conducted under a fixed ratio 1 schedule of reinforcement.
source: At all times, insertion of both active and inactive levers signaled the start of a once daily operant conditioning session conducted under a fixed ratio 1 schedule of reinforcement.
evidence: This describes the reinforcement schedule used in the study.

claim: During the operant conditioning session, a press on the active lever resulted in a single delivery of 0.2 ml of either sweet solution containing 3% glucose and 0.125% saccharin dissolved in water or plain water into the drinking well.
source: During this session, a press on the active lever resulted in a single delivery of 0.2 ml of either sweet solution containing 3% glucose and 0.125% saccharin dissolved in water ('glucose & saccharin') or plain water ('water') into the drinking well.
evidence: This describes the reward delivery procedure.

claim: In pilot experiments, the combination of glucose and saccharin produced more robust operant responding than solutions containing either glucose or saccharin alone.
source: In our pilot experiments (data not included), this combination of glucose and saccharin produced more robust operant responding than solutions containing either glucose or saccharin alone.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the specific reward composition based on pilot data.

claim: Each delivery of either sweet solution or water was paired with 5s illumination of the light-cue signaling a 5s time-out period.
source: Each delivery of either sweet solution or water was paired with 5s illumination of the light-cue signaling a 5s time-out period.
evidence: This describes the cue-pairing procedure.

claim: During the 5s time-out period, presses on the active lever were recorded but without a scheduled consequence.
source: During the 5s time-out period, presses on the active lever were recorded but without a scheduled consequence.
evidence: This describes the time-out procedure.

claim: At all times, presses on the inactive lever were recorded but without a scheduled consequence.
source: At all times, presses on the inactive lever were recorded but without a scheduled consequence.
evidence: This describes the control lever procedure.

claim: Throughout the course of the behavioral model, the rats were repeatedly subjected to habituation periods (both between-sessions and within-sessions) in order to minimize the neurobehavioral impact of environmental cues other than those manipulated experimentally.
source: Throughout the course of this model, the rats were repeatedly subjected to habituation periods (both between-sessions and within-sessions) in order to minimize the neurobehavioral impact of environmental cues (e.g., experimenters and chambers) other than those manipulated experimentally (i.e., active lever, light-cue, S+ and S-).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the habituation procedures.

claim: Three different cohorts of rats were subjected to the entire behavioral procedure (i.e., three biological replicates).
source: Three different cohorts of rats were subjected to the entire behavioral procedure (i.e., three biological replicates).
evidence: This describes the replication structure of the study.

claim: During the self-administration training phase, each rat was required to satisfy two pre-set training criteria: a minimum of five weeks of training (35 sessions), and a minimum of 100 deliveries of the sweet solution for three consecutive sessions.
source: Each rat was required to satisfy two pre-set training criteria: a minimum of five weeks of training (35 sessions), and a minimum of 100 deliveries of the sweet solution for three consecutive sessions.
evidence: This describes the training criteria for the self-administration phase.

claim: Three rats did not satisfy the self-administration training criteria within six weeks of training and were excluded.
source: Three rats that did not satisfy these criteria within six weeks of training were excluded.
evidence: This reports exclusions based on training performance.

claim: During the self-administration training phase, the insertion of the active lever and the illumination of the light-cue predicted the availability of the sweet solution 100% of the time.
source: During this phase, the insertion of the active lever and the illumination of the light-cue predicted the availability of the sweet solution 100% of the time.
evidence: This describes the contingency during the self-administration training phase.

claim: During the discrimination training phase, each rat was required to satisfy three preset training criteria: a minimum of 13 weeks of training (i.e., 46 S+ sessions and 46 S- sessions), a minimum of 50 deliveries of the sweet solution for three consecutive S+ sessions, and a maximum of five deliveries of water for three consecutive S- sessions.
source: Each rat was required to satisfy three preset training criteria: a minimum of 13 weeks of training (i.e., 46 S+ sessions and 46 S- sessions), a minimum of 50 deliveries of the sweet solution for three consecutive S+ sessions, and a maximum of five deliveries of water for three consecutive S- sessions.
evidence: This describes the training criteria for the discrimination training phase.

claim: Nine rats did not satisfy the discrimination training criteria within 14 weeks of training and were excluded.
